title: Windows Certificate Expiration
exclusions: Inventories X.509 certificates present in the explicitly configured `Cert:\LocalMachine\My` and `Cert:\LocalMachine\WebHosting` stores and reports a currently valid certificate when its `NotAfter` instant is at or before the next 30 days, including already expired entries. Presence in a store does not prove that IIS, HTTP.sys, Remote Desktop, AD FS, SQL Server, LDAPS, WinRM, an application, or any remote endpoint is bound to or serving that certificate; binding and live TLS-handshake validation are separate controls. This use case does not discover certificates in CurrentUser, service-account, Java, OpenSSL, appliance, cloud-secret, file-only, HSM, Kubernetes, or other stores; validate chains, revocation, private-key accessibility, EKU, hostname, trust, cryptographic strength, renewal ownership, or replacement deployment; renew, bind, delete, export, or modify certificates; or attest regulatory compliance. Microsoft exposes `NotAfter` in local time and the collector converts it to a UTC epoch; an incorrect host clock or timezone can therefore corrupt urgency. The 30-day threshold, daily cadence, selected stores, freshness limit, ownership policy, and notification severity are local policy, not Microsoft or Splunk defaults. Missing, partial, duplicate, stale, malformed, or count-inconsistent snapshots are telemetry failures and must never mean that no certificate is expiring.
evidence: After deployment, retain the version-controlled `TA_windows_certificate_inventory` collector and hash; approved store list, host inventory, ownership/binding lookup, execution identity, deployment assignment, and effective scripted-input/props settings; one complete manifest plus its exact certificate rows; the `windows_certificate_expiration` saved-search definition, ACL, schedule, dispatch history, and result rows; source-health output for absent, partial, duplicate, malformed, future, or stale snapshots; Windows certificate-manager or PowerShell comparisons; threshold and exception approvals; notification and incident dispositions; and dated positive, negative, boundary, duplicate, freshness, and replacement controls. Result evidence must preserve computer, store, thumbprint, subject, issuer, serial number, `NotBefore`, `NotAfter`, snapshot identity/age, seconds and days remaining, ownership, and expiration state. This documentation-only editorial review created no Windows certificate, private-key, scripted-input, Splunk search, alert, dashboard, or production evidence and does not prove a certificate is bound, trusted, renewable, or safe to remove.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated index with a fixed clock, ingest one schema-1 manifest for `computer_id=win-cert-positive`, `snapshot_complete=1`, `expected_certificate_count=4`, `max_snapshot_age_hours=30`, and exactly four unique certificate rows from the same snapshot. Use integer UTC epochs and reconciled identities for: an active certificate expiring in exactly 30 days, an active certificate expiring in 6.5 days, an active certificate whose `NotAfter` equals the fixed clock, and an active certificate expiring in 30 days plus one second. Expect exactly three rows: states `expiring`, `expiring`, and `expired`; the exact-30-day and exact-expiry boundaries qualify, while the plus-one-second certificate does not. Assert the original store/thumbprint, subject, issuer, snapshot fields, `seconds_remaining`, and rounded `days_remaining`.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Run isolated variants and expect zero primary rows for each invalid snapshot: no manifest; two manifests; `snapshot_complete=0`; expected count unequal to certificate-event count; duplicate store/thumbprint identity; two newest snapshot IDs tied at one epoch; missing computer/store/thumbprint/subject/issuer; and nonnumeric, fractional, zero, or reversed validity epochs. Also expect zero for a complete fresh snapshot containing only a certificate expiring in 30 days plus one second, a not-yet-valid replacement even when its `NotAfter` is near, and a certificate in an uncollected store because no event exists. A snapshot exactly 30 hours old is accepted and one older by one second is rejected. A bounded exception may suppress notification after the base result but must not alter result count or hide source-health failures.

dataSources: Primary source: a deployment-owned Windows PowerShell inventory collector reads `System.Security.Cryptography.X509Certificates.X509Certificate2` objects through the Microsoft Certificate provider from the explicitly approved `Cert:\LocalMachine\My` and `Cert:\LocalMachine\WebHosting` paths. Once daily it emits one JSON `manifest` and one JSON `certificate` event per store/thumbprint identity to local conventions `index=windows`, `source=windows_certificate_inventory`, `sourcetype=ms:windows:certificate`, schema version 1. Required embedded fields are listed in `requiredFields`; `not_before_epoch` and `not_after_epoch` are integer UTC epochs converted from the provider's local-time properties. A Splunk scripted or PowerShell input running on the Windows collection instance transports stdout. IIS/HTTP.sys bindings, remote TLS probes, certificate-authority records, and CMDB ownership are optional correlation sources, not part of the primary expiration denominator.
app: A version-controlled deployment app such as `TA_windows_certificate_inventory` supplies the read-only PowerShell collector, JSON parsing, complete-snapshot source-health search, saved search, dashboard, tests, and bounded exception lookup. It runs under the local Splunk forwarder service identity only after that identity's read access to the selected machine stores is qualified. Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows is not required for this custom certificate feed, and the Universal Forwarder is transport software rather than a Splunkbase app. No premium Splunk app is required.

description: Reports active certificates in each Windows host's approved machine stores when the certificate's exact UTC `NotAfter` instant is no more than 30 days away or has passed. It accepts only a fresh, complete, count-reconciled inventory snapshot and preserves store/thumbprint identity instead of treating a subject name as unique.
value: Certificates that expire before replacement and rebinding can interrupt HTTPS, mutual authentication, federation, directory, remote-management, and application traffic. A complete host/store inventory with exact expiry boundaries gives service owners enough lead time to identify the real binding and renewal path while preventing stale or partial collection from masquerading as a healthy estate.
implementation: Deploy a governed `TA_windows_certificate_inventory` app to in-scope Windows collection hosts. Enumerate only approved LocalMachine stores once daily, convert `NotBefore` and `NotAfter` to UTC epochs, and emit an atomic logical snapshot consisting of one manifest and one event per store/thumbprint. Validate manifest counts and source freshness before saving `windows_certificate_expiration`; run it hourly, alert on any result, route ownership through a post-result lookup, and keep live binding/handshake validation and source health as separate controls.
visualization: Dashboard `Windows — Certificate Expiration`: place expected hosts without a fresh complete snapshot, rejected snapshots, and duplicate identities first. Then show tiles for expired, <=7-day, <=14-day, and <=30-day certificates; a timeline by `not_after_utc`; a stacked count by store and owner; and a table sorted by `seconds_remaining` with computer, store, thumbprint, subject, issuer, DNS names, private-key presence, owner/service, snapshot age, and exception state. Drill down to the raw snapshot, Windows Certificate Manager/PowerShell object, approved binding inventory, and an independently observed TLS handshake. Never label a store certificate as actively served or a missing host as having zero expiring certificates.
schema: Custom complete Windows X509Certificate2 machine-store inventory snapshot
dataModelAcceleration: Not applicable. CIM Change does not define a certificate-inventory dataset and cannot preserve complete-snapshot manifest count, store location/name, thumbprint, `NotBefore`, `NotAfter`, or freshness semantics. At scale, a governed summary index may retain the latest accepted row per computer/store/thumbprint only if it separately preserves manifest acceptance, snapshot identity, source-health failures, and regression parity with the raw search.

knownFalsePositives:
A result is a true statement about `NotAfter` in the accepted machine-store snapshot. “False positive” means the stored certificate is not the active production credential, renewal is already controlled, or the local 30-day policy is not the right notification policy—not that the expiration instant is false.

1. **Renewed certificate is staged alongside the old certificate** — IIS, HTTP.sys, AD FS, SQL Server, LDAPS, or an application can retain the old certificate while a newer replacement is installed. Compare exact store/thumbprint to `netsh http show sslcert`, IIS binding configuration, the service's configuration, and a remote handshake. Suppress only the obsolete thumbprint for a bounded removal window; never suppress by subject alone.

2. **Expired or superseded certificate retained for rollback, decryption, signature verification, or forensics** — Removing an old certificate, especially one with a private key, can break data recovery or evidence validation. Require named owner, retention purpose, ticket, store/thumbprint, and review date. Route it as governed inventory debt rather than deleting it from an alert action.

3. **Autoenrollment or ACME renewal is expected but not yet bound** — A renewal task may normally issue a replacement near expiry, but successful issuance does not prove service binding or handshake cutover. Correlate certificate-enrollment events, task status, replacement thumbprint, binding, service reload, and external probe. Keep paging if the cutover evidence is absent inside the approved lead-time boundary.

4. **Template or test certificate in a production machine store** — Development, enrollment tests, cluster validation, and vendor installers can place short-lived certificates in `My` or `WebHosting`. Confirm EKU, SAN, issuer/template, service binding, environment owner, and ticket. Prefer moving test assets to isolated hosts/stores; otherwise use an exact bounded exception.

5. **Duplicate certificate in multiple selected stores** — The same thumbprint can legitimately exist in both `My` and `WebHosting`. This use case treats store/thumbprint as distinct inventory instances, so both rows can appear. Verify whether both copies have separate consumers; do not deduplicate across stores until ownership and binding are proven.

6. **Hostname/subject suggests service use but no active binding exists** — Subject and DNS SANs describe names, not deployment state. Conversely, a service can select a certificate by thumbprint without an obvious friendly name. Always distinguish with the binding authority and a live endpoint handshake; do not suppress based on CN text matching alone.

7. **Host clock or timezone is wrong** — Because Microsoft exposes `NotAfter` as local time and the collector converts to UTC, a bad clock/timezone can shift urgency. Compare the certificate's raw encoded validity with a trusted inspection tool, Windows Time status, timezone, and Splunk `_time`. Repair time and rerun inventory; do not compensate by changing threshold.

8. **Approved disaster-recovery, blue/green, or offline instance** — A powered-down standby may retain a certificate scheduled for replacement only during activation. Confirm recovery plan, last successful restore/test, network isolation, owner, and next exercise. An offline role still needs a renewal plan; exceptions must expire before activation.

**Safe notification suppression:** apply `windows_certificate_exceptions.csv` only after the base result. Key it by exact `computer_id,store_location,store_name,thumbprint,policy_id` and require numeric inclusive `valid_from_epoch`, exclusive `valid_until_epoch`, owner, approver, ticket, reason, and intended disposition. Reject subject/DNS wildcards, host groups, open-ended dates, and exceptions for missing, stale, partial, duplicate, or malformed snapshots. Preserve every result and matched exception.

cost.search_load_notes: One daily manifest plus one compact JSON row per selected machine-store certificate. The hourly search scans about 40 hours and performs bounded per-host snapshot reconciliation before filtering to the 30-day window.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and exact validity boundary

Assign Windows, PKI, Splunk collection, service-ownership, and alert-response owners. Inventory certificate authorities and renewal mechanisms, but grant the collector no enrollment, export, private-key, binding, service-control, or certificate-deletion privilege. The selected Splunk service identity needs read access only to the approved LocalMachine stores, the deployment system needs permission to install the signed app, and the search role needs read access to `index=windows` plus saved-search permission. Test the exact Windows, PowerShell/.NET, Universal Forwarder, and Splunk versions outside production; this review executed none of them.

Define scope before collection. The reference paths are `Cert:\LocalMachine\My` and `Cert:\LocalMachine\WebHosting`. Microsoft documents the Certificate provider and its `NotAfter` property, while X509Certificate2 documents that `NotAfter` is the local-time date after which the certificate is no longer valid. Convert both validity values to UTC integer epochs on the originating host. The trigger is exact: a certificate already active (`not_before_epoch<=evaluation_epoch`) qualifies when `not_after_epoch-evaluation_epoch<=2,592,000` seconds. Exactly 30 days qualifies; 30 days plus one second does not. At `NotAfter` the row is `expired`. `days_remaining` is rounded display data only; decisions use seconds.

A store object is not a service binding. Subject, SAN, EKU, friendly name, and private-key presence are context and cannot prove the credential is served, trusted, usable, or owned. Build a separate governed binding/owner lookup and, where availability matters, a remote TLS probe. Never delete or renew a certificate from this alert.

## Step 1 — Build a complete read-only snapshot collector

Package a signed PowerShell script in `TA_windows_certificate_inventory\bin`. Start one run with a UUID snapshot ID and UTC epoch, enumerate every certificate from each explicit store, and emit one JSON line per `(store_location,store_name,thumbprint)`. Normalize thumbprints by removing spaces and uppercasing; do not use subject or serial number as identity. Preserve subject, issuer, serial, friendly name, private-key-presence boolean, DNS names, EKU OIDs, and both validity epochs. Do not export private keys, certificate raw bytes, passwords, or key-container ACLs.

Buffer rows in memory or a protected temporary file. Emit the manifest only after every configured store completes and every row validates. Its `expected_certificate_count` must equal emitted certificate rows and distinct identities. Any access failure, provider exception, unreadable certificate, duplicate identity, conversion failure, or partial write must omit `snapshot_complete=1` and produce a separately classified collector error. A zero-certificate snapshot is valid only if all configured stores were successfully enumerated and the manifest count is zero.

The `scriptExample` is an illustrative core, not a claim of production validation. Production code must use strict error handling, log the configured stores and script version, prevent overlapping runs, cap memory, safely serialize unusual subject characters, and ensure one invocation cannot mix computer identities. Sign and hash it under change control.

## Step 2 — Configure Splunk collection and JSON parsing

Prefer a normal scripted input with a `.cmd` wrapper that launches Windows PowerShell noninteractively and returns JSON lines on stdout. Splunk documents that scripted inputs run on an interval and can set index, source, and source type. In the deployment app's `local\inputs.conf` use:

```ini
[script://$SPLUNK_HOME\etc\apps\TA_windows_certificate_inventory\bin\collect-certificates.cmd]
disabled = 0
interval = 0 17 * * *
index = windows
source = windows_certificate_inventory
sourcetype = ms:windows:certificate
```

Splunk's interval semantics allow seconds or cron; cron does not run at startup. Choose a UTC/local schedule deliberately and prevent overlap if enumeration can exceed a day. On Splunk Cloud, the script still runs on a customer-managed Windows forwarder and forwards output; it does not execute in the managed search tier.

On the required parsing/search tiers configure one JSON object per event:

```ini
[ms:windows:certificate]
SHOULD_LINEMERGE = false
LINE_BREAKER = ([\r\n]+)
KV_MODE = json
TRUNCATE = 32768
```

Set `TRUNCATE` above measured maximum row size. Confirm no indexed JSON plus search-time JSON combination creates duplicate values. Verify effective settings with `splunk btool inputs list --debug` and `splunk btool props list ms:windows:certificate --debug`, app placement, index permissions, output queues, and the scheduled script's exit/error records.

## Step 3 — Establish source health before expiration alerting

Maintain `windows_certificate_expected_hosts.csv` with canonical `computer_id`, owner, environment, enabled/retired epochs, and policy ID. A dedicated health search must report an expected host with no run by deadline; no or multiple manifest; incomplete manifest; expected/actual/distinct count mismatch; duplicate identity; future or stale epoch; tied newest snapshots; missing field; malformed JSON; noninteger or reversed validity; unknown store; script overlap; collector error; indexing delay; and forwarder loss. Alert these to PKI/Splunk owners. An empty expiration search is not health evidence.

Spot-check raw rows and require one manifest and exact row count per host/snapshot. Compare selected stores with:

```powershell
Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\My
Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\WebHosting
```

In `certlm.msc`, compare **Certificates (Local Computer) > Personal > Certificates** and **Web Hosting > Certificates** on the same host. Match exact thumbprint and local NotAfter, then confirm the exported UTC epoch formats to the same instant. Differences can result from store scope, permissions, run timing, timezone, or a certificate added after the snapshot; document exact comparison bounds.

## Step 4 — Create and understand the expiration search

Save the catalogue SPL as `windows_certificate_expiration`; schedule hourly and trigger when result count exceeds zero. The 40-hour search horizon allows a daily run with 30-hour freshness. The first stages cast every numeric value and establish host/snapshot identity. Conditional fields and `eventstats` require exactly one manifest, one manifest control value, and equality among expected count, event count, and distinct store/thumbprint count before certificate rows survive.

The search selects one newest accepted snapshot per computer and rejects tied newest IDs. It calculates age from the embedded snapshot epoch, rejects future or older-than-policy snapshots, and validates certificate identity plus integer, ordered validity epochs. It then compares exact seconds to 30 days. `not_before_epoch<=evaluation_epoch` prevents a staged replacement that is not yet valid from firing merely because its entire validity period is short. An expired certificate remains visible regardless of how long ago it expired; retention/removal policy belongs to the owner and exception process.

Do not replace this with `Get-ChildItem -ExpiringInDays 30` output alone: Microsoft documents that option, but a filtered collector cannot prove how many nonexpiring objects were successfully examined and makes complete-snapshot reconciliation weaker. Do not add CIM Change `tstats`; certificate presence/expiry is not a CIM Change record.

## Step 5 — Validate boundaries, completeness, and service relevance

Use fixed-time synthetic JSON in an isolated index and assert every `controlTest` output. Run each malformed snapshot variant alone. Test exact 30-day, plus/minus one second, exact expiry, not-yet-valid, snapshot age exact 30 hours, freshness plus one second, duplicate event, duplicate identity across one store, same thumbprint across two stores, unusual Unicode subject, multi-valued SAN/EKU, empty optional arrays, zero-certificate complete run, and host clock ahead/behind. Confirm same thumbprint in two stores produces two valid instances.

On a nonproduction Windows host, import or create only approved test certificates in an isolated selected store, run the collector, compare PowerShell and `certlm.msc`, and remove test material under PKI procedure. Never import a private production key or alter a live binding to test monitoring. Validate IIS or HTTP.sys correlation separately using its approved management surface and a remote handshake. Prove that a replacement store row does not automatically close the old-thumbprint incident until binding/owner evidence says it should.

Record script hash/version, host clock/timezone, store list, snapshot ID/count, raw event IDs, search job, fixed evaluation epoch, expected/actual rows, and operator. Keep `status=draft` until runtime tests, source health, binding/ownership enrichment, alert delivery, RBAC, exception expiry, dashboard, and evidence retention are accepted by Windows, PKI, service, and Splunk owners.

## Step 6 — Operationalize response, suppression, and evidence

Build the dashboard in `visualization`, with source trust first. Route expired and <=7-day rows urgently according to service criticality; 8–14 and 15–30-day states can create planned renewal work. Severity must incorporate confirmed service binding, external exposure, renewal lead time, failover, and owner—not subject text alone. Throttle by exact computer/store/thumbprint/policy while preserving each hourly evaluation.

Responder sequence: verify snapshot freshness/completeness and host time; inspect exact store/thumbprint in PowerShell or Certificate Manager; identify the actual service binding and live served chain; confirm owner, issuer/template, renewal method, replacement order status, and private-key/binding requirements; renew through the approved PKI mechanism; bind/deploy and safely reload the service; validate remote handshake, hostname, chain, and application health; then retire the old certificate only under retention/change policy. Never automatically delete, export, enroll, bind, restart, or change private-key ACLs.

Apply only the exact bounded exception contract in `knownFalsePositives`. Suppress notification, not the base result or health search. Retain evidence under local operational/security policy; the 90-day cost value is advisory, not a compliance mandate. Review stores, cadence, threshold, ownership, collector compatibility, and exception inventory after Windows/PowerShell/forwarder upgrades, PKI or renewal changes, new service platforms, timezone changes, and certificate-store migrations.

## Step 7 — Troubleshoot without hiding unknown state

- **No rows at all:** query the independent expected-host health search, script schedule/exit, app assignment, service identity, stdout, index routing, and JSON parsing. Do not call the estate healthy.
- **Access denied for one store:** verify the collection identity and store ACL/context. Mark the run incomplete; do not emit a complete manifest for stores that succeeded.
- **Count mismatch or duplicates:** inspect overlapping script invocations, repeated stdout, duplicate deployment apps, replay, and identity normalization. Correct collection rather than using arbitrary `dedup`.
- **NotAfter differs by hours:** compare local timezone, Windows Time, X509Certificate2 local-time value, UTC conversion, and epoch formatting. Do not subtract a fixed offset.
- **Certificate visible in `certlm.msc` but absent:** verify Local Computer versus Current User, exact store, service-account context, collector store list, archived visibility, and timing. Expand scope only through a tested policy revision.
- **Alert remains after renewal:** a replacement does not mutate the old object. Verify new thumbprint and actual binding; then remove or boundedly except the old certificate under owner approval.
- **Remote endpoint serves a different certificate:** the endpoint may terminate on a load balancer, proxy, cluster peer, container, or cloud service. Correct the binding inventory and deploy a separate remote probe; do not relabel the local row as the served credential.
- **Snapshot is stale:** inspect script runtime/overlap, forwarder queues, host availability, index delay, and schedule timezone. Never increase freshness merely to make the alert return old data.
- **CIM search is empty:** expected; no CIM model is claimed. Use this custom contract or a purpose-built summary that retains its manifest and validity semantics.
grandmaExplanation: We check the identity papers stored on each Windows computer and warn before one reaches its final valid moment. That gives the team time to find the service that uses it and replace it before people or machines lose access.
hardware: Windows Server and Windows client systems on which the deployed collection identity can read the explicitly approved `LocalMachine` certificate stores. Remote appliances, non-Windows hosts, containers, CurrentUser/service-account stores, HSM-backed inventories, cloud key vaults, and file-based keystores require separate collectors and identity contracts.
scriptExample:
```powershell
# Illustrative collector core; production code must add try/catch, atomic run logging, signing, and tests.
$SnapshotId = [guid]::NewGuid().ToString()
$SnapshotEpoch = [DateTimeOffset]::UtcNow.ToUnixTimeSeconds()
$ComputerId = $env:COMPUTERNAME.ToLowerInvariant()
$Rows = @()
foreach ($StoreName in @('My','WebHosting')) {
  Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath "Cert:\LocalMachine\$StoreName" | ForEach-Object {
    $Cert = $_
    $Rows += [ordered]@{
      schema_version=1; record_type='certificate'; computer_id=$ComputerId
      snapshot_id=$SnapshotId; snapshot_epoch=$SnapshotEpoch
      store_location='LocalMachine'; store_name=$StoreName
      thumbprint=($Cert.Thumbprint -replace ' ','').ToUpperInvariant()
      subject=$Cert.Subject; issuer=$Cert.Issuer; serial_number=$Cert.SerialNumber
      friendly_name=$Cert.FriendlyName; has_private_key=[bool]$Cert.HasPrivateKey
      dns_names=@($Cert.DnsNameList | ForEach-Object { $_.Unicode })
      eku_oids=@($Cert.EnhancedKeyUsageList | ForEach-Object { $_.ObjectId.Value })
      not_before_epoch=([DateTimeOffset]$Cert.NotBefore).ToUniversalTime().ToUnixTimeSeconds()
      not_after_epoch=([DateTimeOffset]$Cert.NotAfter).ToUniversalTime().ToUnixTimeSeconds()
    }
  }
}
$Rows | ForEach-Object { $_ | ConvertTo-Json -Compress -Depth 5 }
[ordered]@{schema_version=1;record_type='manifest';computer_id=$ComputerId;snapshot_id=$SnapshotId;snapshot_epoch=$SnapshotEpoch;snapshot_complete=1;expected_certificate_count=$Rows.Count;max_snapshot_age_hours=30} | ConvertTo-Json -Compress
```
